q: According to the Eighth Edition, how is the quality of a deliverable and of its process measured?
options: By how many team members have reviewed and signed it
By acceptance criteria, done criteria and fitness for use
By how closely the work matched the planned schedule
By the sponsor's personal opinion at the handover
explanation: Quality of the deliverable and its processes is measured by conformance to acceptance criteria, the definition of done (DoD), fitness for use and overall efficiency.

q: Which effort focuses on deliverables meeting the defined specifications, through product design, testing and the handling of defects?
explanation: Quality control is about creating deliverables that meet defined specifications and thresholds; related concepts are product design, testing and defects. Quality assurance is about using the processes effectively.

q: Every deliverable passes its tests, but the PMO finds that the team skipped two required review steps. Which effort found the problem?
options: Quality assurance, which looks at the processes
Quality control, which tests the deliverables
Validate Scope, which formally accepts them
explanation: Quality assurance is about using project processes effectively and following standards; its related concepts include compliance and audits. Here the deliverables were fine, but the process was not followed.

q: In the Eighth Edition, which process updates the quality management plan and uses test and inspection planning?
explanation: Figure 2-14 shows Plan Scope Management with test and inspection planning among its tools, and updates to the scope, quality and requirements management plans among its outputs.

q: A shipping company entering a new market learns that its major retailers have stricter packaging standards than the regulator. What does the quality principle suggest?
options: Meet only the regulator's rules, as they are the law
Meet the stricter standards to exceed expectations
Ask the regulator to raise its standards first
Leave packaging out of the quality requirements
explanation: In the principle in action, a quality-driven approach looks at the wider stakeholder system. Meeting the customers' higher standards satisfies the law and exceeds expectations, strengthening market entry.

q: After a power cut, the new ticket kiosks restart and are back in service within a minute, with no data lost. Which quality dimension does this show?
explanation: Resilience asks whether deliverables and processes cope with unforeseen failures and recover quickly. Reliability is about consistency; conformity about specifications; uniformity about parity across outputs.

q: Which of these is a quality metric, as the PMBOK Guide describes it?
options: Errors found per thousand lines of code
The names of all the project's quality auditors
The date of the next steering meeting
explanation: Quality metrics describe attributes and how compliance is verified, for example tasks on time, CPI, failure rates, defects per day, downtime, errors per line of code, satisfaction scores and test coverage.

q: Which of these belongs in a quality management plan?
options: The stakeholders' power and interest levels
explanation: The plan may include quality standards and objectives, roles and responsibilities, deliverables and processes subject to review, planned quality activities, and tools with procedures for nonconformance and continuous improvement.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Quality management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Quality management plan

q: Defects appear somewhere between order entry and shipping. The team wants to see every step and decision point of the process to find where. Which tool fits?
explanation: A flowchart (process map) shows the sequence of steps, decision points, loops and parallel paths of a process, which helps find areas for improvement.

q: The team's defect rate seems high, but it has nothing to compare it with. A partner company in another industry agrees to share its figures and practices. Which technique is the team using?
explanation: Benchmarking compares products, processes and practices with comparable organizations, inside or outside the organization and even in other industries, for ideas and a basis for measuring performance.

q: What is one objective of a quality audit?
options: Assigning the blame for each defect to a team member
Replacing the project's quality control tests
Approving the final deliverables for the customer
explanation: Quality audit objectives include identifying good practices and nonconformities, gaps and shortcomings, sharing good practices, offering help to improve processes, and adding to the lessons learned repository.

q: The sponsor asks what the weekly quality report will give them. Which set is right?
explanation: A quality report includes quality management issues, recommendations for corrective actions, and a summary of findings from quality control activities.
options: The cost baseline, the funding plan and the reserves
The team charter, ground rules and roles
Quality issues, corrective actions and findings

q: Deliverables have passed the team's quality control checks. What are they called now, and what comes next?
options: Accepted deliverables; they move to closing
Approved changes; then the change log
explanation: Monitor and Control Scope produces verified deliverables. Validate Scope then formalizes their acceptance, producing accepted deliverables.

q: The PMO plots the number of scope changes per month on a control chart. What can this show?
options: Whether the change process is stable
The cost of each change to the budget
The approval date of every change
explanation: Control charts determine whether a process is stable or predictable. Besides repetitive production, they can track cost and schedule variances or the frequency of scope changes, to see if project processes are in control.

q: Which of these is a prevention cost?
options: Training the team in a new standard
Inspecting all of the finished goods
explanation: Prevention costs build a quality product: training, documented processes, equipment and time to do it right. Inspection is appraisal; rework is internal failure; warranty repairs are external failure.

q: Customers return a product because of a defect found after launch. Which cost of quality category is this?
explanation: External failure costs come from failures found by the customer: liabilities, warranty work, complaints, returns, lost business and damaged reputation.

q: To save money, the sponsor wants to cut all design reviews and most testing. What does the cost of quality suggest?
options: Do it; appraisal costs never add value
Do it, but only for the deliverables kept internal
Move all testing to after the handover
Failure costs found later will likely be higher
explanation: The optimal cost of quality balances prevention and appraisal against failure. Early inspection and review are good investments; trying to test quality in late usually fails because scrap and rework are costly.

q: How does reducing rework support sustainability, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: It removes any need for a separate quality management plan
It avoids wasted resources and emissions from rework
It moves environmental duties to the supplier
It lets the team skip compliance checks
explanation: Attention to quality reduces the negative impact on the environment, avoiding the unnecessary use of natural resources and emissions due to rework.

q: A defect keeps coming back after each fix. What should the project manager do?
options: Fix it again, but faster next time
Add more inspectors at the very end of the line
Find and remove its root cause in the process
Accept it as a known risk
explanation: Root cause analysis finds the basic reason for a defect. When all root causes are removed, the problem does not recur. More inspection only finds the defect; it does not prevent it.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Root cause analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Root cause analysis

q: Before building each story, the whole team agrees the acceptance criteria and writes the tests for them. Which practice is this?
explanation: In ATDD the entire team discusses the acceptance criteria, then creates the tests, and writes just enough code and automated tests to meet them.
ref: Agile Practice Guide, Software-Centric Approaches and Metrics for Agile Teams

links.label: Agile Practice Guide, Software-Centric Approaches and Metrics for Agile Teams

q: Work from several developers is merged into the whole product many times a day and then retested. Which practice is this?
explanation: Continuous integration is the frequent incorporation of work into the whole, then retesting to check that the entire product still works. It is paired with continuous delivery.

q: How is quality assurance usually performed in predictive and in agile projects?
options: Formally in agile, informally in predictive
Formal in predictive; formal or informal in agile
Never in agile projects, since the team tests its own work
Only by an external auditor in both
explanation: In predictive projects QA is usually formal, as strong process quality minimizes variance. In agile or adaptive projects it can be formal or informal, depending on the context.

q: Which cost of quality category are the technicians' repair visits to the branches?
explanation: The faults reached the customer, so the repairs are external failure costs, like warranty work and complaints. Finding them in the vendor's tests before shipping would have been internal failure.

q: What should the project manager do about the PMO audit's finding on the skipped security test?
options: Ignore it, since every kiosk has already passed acceptance
Correct the process and raise a change request if needed
Replace the PMO auditor with a team member
Remove the security test from the plan
explanation: A quality audit identifies nonconformities so the process can be improved. Manage Quality Assurance produces change requests and plan updates; the agreed test is part of the quality management plan and must be followed or formally changed.

q: The team wants to find out why most of the card-reader faults happen. Which tool should it use first?
explanation: A cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram breaks down the possible causes of a problem into branches, to trace the effect back to its root cause.

q: Which TWO are part of the cost of conformance?
explanation: Prevention and appraisal are money spent during the project to avoid failures (cost of conformance). Internal and external failure are the cost of nonconformance.

q: Which THREE are tools and techniques of the Manage Quality Assurance process?
explanation: Figure 2-7 lists audits, checklists, data representation (affinity diagrams, cause-and-effect diagrams, flowcharts), decision-making, problem-solving and process improvement.

q: Which TWO practices help an agile team build quality into its work?
options: Testing at all levels, mostly automated
A definition of done for each increment
Testing only at the end of the release
explanation: Agile teams test at all levels with a strong preference for automated tests, and keep a definition of done for every increment. Without attention to quality, it soon becomes impossible to release rapidly.

q: Match each cost of quality category with its examples.
explanation: Prevention builds a quality product; appraisal assesses it; internal failures are found by the project; external failures are found by the customer.

q: Complete each statement about quality.

blanks.text: Using the processes effectively and following standards is
Making deliverables meet their specifications through testing is
Verified deliverables are formally accepted in

explanation: Quality assurance looks at the processes, quality control at the deliverables, and Validate Scope formalizes acceptance.
